intention: The ground loop outlives the terminal that started it: a heartbeat spawned by an entry point is parented on the user manager, not on the caller's cgroup, so killing the window or the session leaves it beating.
why: The heartbeat is the one resident process every callback in the system hangs off, and today its lifetime is an accident of which window launched it. MEASURED 2026-08-18: the kernel oom-killed the claude binary at 14:57:31; systemd marked app-org.kde.konsole-b1d62b21cfc74a57b8e15d874590bdc6.scope 'Failed with result oom-kill' at 14:57:43; the loop's own trail at ~/.cairn/logs/ground_loop/0/diagnostics.jsonl carries exactly three loop starts that day - 14:52:55, 14:58:01, 15:33:34 - so the heartbeat died in that scope kill with nothing between. It died the same way on 2026-08-10 ('74,209 beats, then nothing, and nothing was loud about it'). A thing declared ALWAYS UP whose survival depends on a terminal staying open is policy wearing physics' clothes.
how: Replace the `setsid python3 -m cairn.devices.ground_loop` spawn at launchers/superclaude:229 with a transient user unit: `systemd-run --user --unit=cairn-ground-loop --working-directory=<repo> -p StandardOutput=append:$HOME/.cairn/logs/ground_loop_nohup.log -p StandardError=append:<same> -- python3 -m cairn.devices.ground_loop`. It lands at /user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/cairn-ground-loop.service - a SIBLING of the Konsole scope and of the session scope rather than a child of either. Everything else about the spawn is unchanged: still spawn-blind (the singleton guard decides), still under the prime directive with a guarded fall-through to today's setsid spawn when systemd-run is missing or its probe fails, still `|| true`, and the boot log names which branch it took, exactly as the memory-scope block already does at :291/:302. The StandardOutput redirect is load-bearing, not decoration: a unit does not inherit the shell's append redirect, and without it the losing claimant's refusal - the line that distinguishes 'refused, one is running' from 'broke' - vanishes into the journal.
traces_to: Law 4 first - a rule that matters is enforced by physics, not policy. 'The ground loop is always up' (Akien, 2026-08-11) is enforced today by nobody closing the window. Law 3 - the survival was never measured, only intended, and the word 'setsid' in the spawn's own comment was read as evidence of it. And the founding aim of getting Akien out of running the system: a heartbeat that dies with a terminal is a thing only a human notices, and on 2026-08-18 a human did.
gates: code-seam invariant, transcribed: PROVED, and feeds-back-to-origin-on-failure (Laws 3 + 8). PROVE GATE: the tester runs launchers/proofs/test_ground_loop_survives_its_caller.py, verdict and seal from the same hand. Its non-hollow tooth is that it asks the KERNEL - /proc/<pid>/cgroup for the spawned loop, then kills the caller's whole process tree and reads the loop's own trail for beats on both sides of the kill - rather than reading flags back out of the launcher script. The precedent is launchers/proofs/test_superclaude_memory_scope.py, which drives the real launcher through a pty and asks the kernel for the limits. DURABILITY GATE: not done until tested AND committed to git.
falsifier: DONE when the loop, started through the launcher, sits in a cgroup that is neither the caller's nor a descendant of it - asked of the kernel, never read off the launcher's flags - AND survives its caller's entire process tree being killed, with the loop's own trail showing an unbroken run of beats across that kill, AND the losing-claimant refusal still lands in ~/.cairn/logs/ground_loop_nohup.log rather than only in the journal. WRONG INTENT if: (1) anything becomes system-level startup - an installed unit file, an `enable`, anything surviving a reboot (Akien's 2026-08-11 ruling); (2) the launcher grows an opinion about whether a loop is already running, re-deriving the singleton guard at the caller (Law 1, and guard.py's own docstring names this caller); (3) the spawn can abort, delay or fail a launch (the prime directive: from parse to exec, nothing may stop a session starting).
horizon: one launch. Every clause is answerable at the first superclaude boot after the change - no clock, no live host, no wait.
parent: none - it is not a child of an-entry-point-starts-the-loop-only-once. That node owns WHETHER a second loop starts and is PROVED; this one owns how long the first one lives, and neither contains the other.
children: none, because it is a leaf: one seam (the spawn at launchers/superclaude:229), one owner (the launcher), one proof. The sibling that could look like a child is named rather than absorbed - the sudo relay died in the same scope kill with the same parenting defect, but it has a different start path and is Akien's privileged act, and folding it in would put a more specific thing inside a less specific one (his ruling, 2026-08-18). It wants its own node.

watchme.trigger: every beat - the loop reads its own /proc/self/cgroup, which it is already awake to do; no clock of its own, no scan, one file read of ~200 bytes. Deliberately not a launch-time check: a launch-time check answers 'was it started right', and the question is 'is it parented right NOW', which is the one that was false and unnoticed.
watchme.enough: NOT satisfied by the launch that installs it. Enough when it has seen at least one caller die while the loop kept beating - until then the watch has confirmed only that the parenting is what the launcher said, never that the parenting does what it is for.
watchme.carrier: a verdict artifact against this ticket's falsifier: the cgroup path the kernel reports, whether it is a descendant of a terminal or session scope, and the beat number - so a reader can join a survival to the kill that preceded it.
watchme.nexus: the ground_loop device's own tree - the same nexus its liveness and staleness watches teach, this being another fact about the loop's residency rather than about any caller.
watchme.consumer: the trouble lane on a red (a heartbeat that has quietly become a child of a terminal again is exactly the class of thing that stays true and unnoticed for days), and the ground_loop pane for the standing green.

provenance: Born 2026-08-18 at Akien's 'restarted.' and his 'yes you can restart it. just do the whole not-connected-to-this-window thing' - the restart he authorised is what made the parenting visible, because doing it by hand meant choosing a parent and therefore noticing that the launcher does not. The first framing given to him was wrong (a regression from the memory-cap commit 124442b) and was corrected before the cast: the spawn sits 60 lines above the exec-into-scope, so the loop never lands in the session scope and never did.

distinctions_recorded.against_akiens_no_system_level_startup_r: His 2026-08-11 ruling reads 'THE INTENTION IS THE GROUND LOOP IS ALWAYS UP. IF ITS NOT UP, LAUNCHING AN ENTRY POINT LAUNCHES IT. NO SYSTEM LEVEL STARTUP REQUIRED.' Taking the why of each side: his is that nobody should have to install or remember anything for the heartbeat to be up. This node's is that the heartbeat must not die when a window does. Not exclusive, not terminal, so a DISTINCTION: a transient systemd-run --user unit installs no file, survives no reboot, and is still started by an entry point launching. What changes is the spawned process's PARENT, not who starts it or when. THE EDGE, and it is his to rule on: if he meant the ruling to name the MECHANISM (nothing systemd-shaped anywhere) and not only the outcome, this node dies.
distinctions_recorded.against_host_seam_installer: That node projects declared apply/verify recipes over a machine's host-seams - which is what an INSTALLED unit would need and a transient one does not. The two do not touch.
distinctions_recorded.setsid_detaches_the_tty_not_the_cgroup: MEASURED 2026-08-18 rather than reasoned: a setsid'd child spawned from this session reported the identical cgroup path as its parent. The spawn's own comment - 'setsid so it outlives this shell and the terminal' - is half true, and the false half is the half that mattered.

open_at_cast: UNPROVEN and carried into the build as its one open question: that `systemd-run --user --unit=<name>` fails harmlessly when the unit name is already taken. The spawn is deliberately blind and the singleton guard is what refuses a second loop; if systemd-run instead errors before the guard can run, the spawn's blindness changes shape. A five-second measurement at BUILDME, written into the falsifier rather than left in prose.
